stances.claim: Japanese law requiring married couples to share a single surname is a 'bastion of masculinity' driving ~30% of common-law couples to avoid marriage, including 40% among 20-year-olds.
PH Civil Code Article 370 gives a married woman three name options; an informal hyphenated form is widely tolerated though not in the Code.

'Mrs. Maria Castillo' is grammatically inaccurate because 'Mrs.' is the abbreviation of 'Mistress' -- strictly, she is mistress of Juan, not of Maria; a parenthetical (Mrs.) would be more literally accurate, though usage now tolerates it.
stances.rhetorical_move: etymological pedantry softened by usage-tolerance concession

stances.claim: Married women are traditionally allowed to continue using their maiden names, especially where professional licenses or public recognition were earned in the single name.

Under Article 371, the guilty party in an annulled or void marriage reverts to her single name; the innocent party retains options including her husband's surname unless the court decrees otherwise or remarriage intervenes.

Women already dominate trial courts (56%), the CTA (77%), the CA (45%), and the Sandiganbayan (35%), but comprise only 13% of the Supreme Court (2 of 15), shrinking further with J. Lazaro-Javier's November 16, 2026 retirement.
Women soon outnumbering men in the legal profession is not a bad idea because it will push men to work harder, scrutinize details more closely, and prepare for trial more avidly.

one_paragraph_summary: Sparked by a Kyodo News item that nearly 30% of Japanese in common-law relationships avoid marriage to preserve their own or a partner's surname (40% among 20-year-olds), Panganiban surveys the names married women may use under the Civil Code of the Philippines. Article 370 offers three options -- maiden name + maiden surname + husband's surname (with a widely tolerated hyphenated form), maiden name + husband's surname, or husband's full name prefixed by 'Mrs.' -- paired with an etymological caveat that 'Mrs.' is the abbreviation of 'Mistress' so strictly 'Mrs. Maria Castillo' is inaccurate, though usage now tolerates it. Married women may also continue using their maiden names, especially where professional licenses, passports, or driver's licenses were earned in the single name; his own youngest daughter, Maria Evelyn Panganiban, still does. Performers may use pen names and aliases (Kyla, Heart Evangelista, Coco Martin, Dingdong Dantes). Widows may continue the married name, revert to the maiden name, or chain mother's-and-father's-and-deceased-husband's surnames (his cousin Evelyn Santos Camus Alcantara illustrates the pattern), and remarried widows may chain first and second husbands' surnames (Boots Anson Roa Rodrigo). Article 371 governs annulled and void marriages: the guilty party reverts to her single name; the innocent party may resume her single name or retain the husband's surname unless the court decrees otherwise or remarriage intervenes. Citing CJ Gesmundo's recent speech, he reports women make up 56% of trial judges, 77% of the CTA, 45% of the CA, and 35% of the Sandiganbayan, but only 13% (2 of 15) of the Supreme Court -- soon to drop further with J. Amy C. Lazaro-Javier's November 16, 2026 retirement. He closes with a 1960 bar-review-class anecdote in which the reviewer dismissed the fewer-than-10 ladies in a 100-student class -- 'guffaw from the men but grit and smirk from the women' -- and his prediction that women soon outnumbering men in the profession will make the men work harder, scrutinize more closely, and prepare for trial more avidly.
